lessons.title: Body systems and how a healthy animal works
lessons.html:
Body systems and how a healthy animal works

A supervisor who understands how an animal's body works can spot problems early, explain treatments to workers and talk sensibly with the vet. This module looks at the body systems that matter most on a livestock farm.

The main systems

  • Skeleton and muscles carry the body and give the meat. Lameness often starts in the hooves, joints or muscles.
  • Respiratory system: nose, windpipe and lungs. Fast, laboured breathing, coughing or nasal discharge point to pneumonia, heat stress or dust.
  • Circulatory system: heart and blood vessels carry oxygen, nutrients and heat. Pale gums and eyelids can mean blood loss or anaemia, for example from wireworm in sheep and goats.
  • Nervous system: brain, spinal cord and nerves. Staggering, circling, blindness or fits mean the nervous system is affected, as with some plant poisonings, heartwater or rabies. Treat any animal with nervous signs as a possible rabies case and do not put your hand in its mouth.
  • Skin and coat protect the body and help control temperature. A dull, staring coat is often the first sign of poor health or poor feeding.

Normal signs

Learn what is normal for your animals so you can recognise what is not. A healthy animal is alert, eats and ruminates, has bright eyes, a shiny coat, normal dung and moves freely with the herd. Temperature is taken rectally with a thermometer. Normal ranges differ between species and between young and adult animals, so use the reference ranges your vet or farm health plan gives you rather than guessing.

Homeostasis

The body works hard to keep its temperature, water and salt balance steady. In very hot weather animals pant, sweat (cattle) and seek shade; they drink much more water. When water or shade is short, this balance breaks down and production drops long before the animal looks sick.

lessons.title: The digestive system: ruminants and monogastrics
lessons.html:
The digestive system: ruminants and monogastrics

Ruminants

Cattle, sheep and goats are ruminants. Their stomach has four parts:

  1. Rumen - a large fermentation vat where microbes break down grass and roughage.
  2. Reticulum - works with the rumen; heavy objects such as wire and nails collect here (hardware disease).
  3. Omasum - absorbs water from the feed.
  4. Abomasum - the true stomach, with acid and enzymes like ours.

Ruminants bring food back up and chew it again (chewing the cud). An animal that stops ruminating is usually sick. The rumen microbes can turn poor veld grass into energy and protein, which is why ruminants do well on extensive farms.

Rumen problems you must know

  • Bloat: gas is trapped in the rumen, often on lush lucerne or clover. The left side swells high up. This is an emergency - call the supervisor or vet at once.
  • Acidosis: too much grain too quickly, for example when cattle arrive at a feedlot or break into the maize store. Change feed slowly over days.

Monogastrics

Pigs and poultry have a simple stomach. They cannot digest much fibre and need concentrated, balanced feed. Poultry have a crop to store food and a gizzard that grinds it with grit. Feed quality and water supply affect their growth almost immediately.

Young ruminants

A newborn calf or lamb works like a monogastric. Milk bypasses the rumen through the oesophageal groove into the abomasum. The rumen develops as the young animal starts to nibble grass and creep feed. This is why weaning too early or too suddenly sets animals back.

lessons.title: Reproduction and growth
lessons.html:
Reproduction and growth

The female

The female reproductive tract consists of the ovaries, oviducts, uterus, cervix and vagina. Females come into heat (oestrus) in a regular cycle. A cow on heat stands to be mounted, is restless and may have clear mucus. Ewes and does show less obvious signs, so farmers use rams or bucks with marking harnesses or crayon to see which females have been served.

Gestation length differs by species: roughly nine months in cattle and about five months in sheep and goats. Ask your farm manager for the exact planning figures used on your farm.

The male

The bull, ram or buck produces sperm in the testes. Fertility is affected by heat, poor condition, injury and disease. Bulls and rams should be examined for breeding soundness by a vet before the breeding season.

Birth and the newborn

Know the signs of a normal birth and when to call for help. If a female has strained for a long time without progress, or a leg or the head is turned back, call your supervisor or vet. Never pull hard on a calf with ropes or a bakkie. Newborns must drink colostrum (first milk) within the first hours of life. It gives antibodies that protect them until their own immunity develops.

Growth and the mammary gland

Young animals grow bone first, then muscle, then fat. Feed shortages during early growth cause lasting damage. The udder is a gland that makes milk from nutrients in the blood. Mastitis is infection of the udder, giving hot, hard quarters and clots in the milk.

Key points

  • Know the normal signs of health so you can spot sick animals early.
  • Ruminants have four stomach compartments; the rumen ferments roughage.
  • Bloat is an emergency; change grain feeding slowly to prevent acidosis.
  • Pigs and poultry need balanced, concentrated feed.
  • Newborns must get colostrum within the first hours.
  • Treat animals with nervous signs as possible rabies cases.
